phases.message: I hold Mom's power of attorney and I look after her retirement accounts. Start in my inbox: her tax preparer, Pinebrook, Harborline, her 401(k), Mom's own note and anything else about her required minimum distributions.

Pinebrook. Read each of Mom's accounts, their 31 December values, what has already come out and Pinebrook's RMD guide. Request whatever she still has to take this year from the account it has to come from, and nothing she doesn't need.

Harborline. Read both of her accounts, including the IRA she inherited from Uncle Walter, the scheduled withdrawals and the guide to inherited IRAs. Correct anything she missed, request what she still owes for this year from the right account, and stop anything that isn't needed.

Docshelf, the folder Wexley & Marr share with us. Read their drafts, the Form 5329 instructions they saved and the payments they set up. Approve what should be filed with her 2025 return, with the waiver if she can ask for it, authorize only what she really has to pay, and tell me what you left alone and why.

pb_rules.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026. An owner's required minimum distributions (RMDs), under IRC 401(a)(9), Treas. Reg. 1.401(a)(9)-5 and -9 and 1.408-8 as amended by the final regulations of July 2024 (applying from 2025), as IRS Publication 590-B and the IRS's RMD pages explain them. For IRAs inherited from someone else, see the inheriting custodian's rules. Topics: start, amount, table, aggregate, plans, roth, joint, extra.

An owner born from 1951 to 1959 takes RMDs from the year she reaches 73; born 1960 or later, from 75 (IRC 401(a)(9)(C)(v), as SECURE 2.0 set it). The first RMD, for the year she reaches 73, may wait until 1 April of the next year, her required beginning date; that next year's own RMD is still due by 31 December, so that one year holds two. Every later RMD is due by 31 December of its own year, with no April option. A 401(k) from an employer she has retired from, and never owned 5% of, starts the same way.

Each account's RMD for a year is its value on 31 December of the year before, divided by the Uniform Lifetime Table's distribution period for the owner's age on her birthday in that year (Treas. Reg. 1.401(a)(9)-5(b) and (c)). It is never figured on today's value. Pinebrook rounds to the cent.
Uniform Lifetime Table (Treas. Reg. 1.401(a)(9)-9(c), the 2022 tables), age: distribution period. 72: 27.4. 73: 26.5. 74: 25.5. 75: 24.6. 76: 23.7. 77: 22.9.

Traditional IRAs she owns: each one's RMD is figured separately, and the total may be taken from any one or more of them (Treas. Reg. 1.408-8(e)). IRAs she holds as a beneficiary are never combined with IRAs she owns: an inherited IRA's RMD is taken only from IRAs inherited from the same person, and a withdrawal from her own IRA never counts toward it.

A 401(k)'s RMD is figured for that plan and taken from that plan alone. An IRA withdrawal never satisfies it, and a 401(k) payment never counts toward an IRA's RMD (IRS RMD FAQs; Form 5329 instructions).
A Roth IRA has no RMD while its owner is alive, and a Roth withdrawal never counts toward a traditional IRA's RMD (Treas. Reg. 1.408-8(e)).

The Joint and Last Survivor Table replaces the Uniform Lifetime Table only when the owner's spouse is her sole beneficiary and more than 10 years younger than she is (Treas. Reg. 1.401(a)(9)-5(c)(2)). Otherwise the Uniform Lifetime Table applies.
Taking more than a year's RMD gives no credit toward a later year's (Treas. Reg. 1.401(a)(9)-5(a)). Nothing beyond the RMD has to be taken.

hl_rules.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026. Inherited IRAs and missed distributions, under IRC 401(a)(9)(B), (E) and (H), the final regulations of July 2024 (T.D. 10001: Treas. Reg. 1.401(a)(9)-5, 1.401(a)(9)-9, 1.408-8 and 54.4974-1, applying from 2025), IRS Notices 2022-53, 2023-54 and 2024-35, and IRC 4974. Topics: beneficiary, ten-year, relief, divisor, table, correction, spouse.

An eligible designated beneficiary is the owner's surviving spouse, his minor child, a disabled or chronically ill person, or a person not more than 10 years younger than the owner (IRC 401(a)(9)(E)(ii)). Any other person named as beneficiary is a designated beneficiary under the 10-year rule.

When the owner died on or after his required beginning date and the beneficiary is a designated beneficiary under the 10-year rule, she takes an RMD every year, starting the year after the death, and the whole account by 31 December of the 10th year after the year of death (Treas. Reg. 1.401(a)(9)-5(d); T.D. 10001). Each year's RMD is due by 31 December of that year.

IRS Notices 2022-53 (for 2021 and 2022), 2023-54 (for 2023) and 2024-35 (for 2024): for those years, the IRS does not assert the excise tax on an RMD not taken under the 10-year rule after an owner died on or after his required beginning date. Those years' RMDs are not made up, and the 10-year deadline does not move. The final regulations apply from 2025: the 2025 RMD and every one after it are required, with no relief.

Each year's RMD is the account's value on 31 December of the year before, divided by the longer of two remaining life expectancies, both from the Single Life Table (Treas. Reg. 1.401(a)(9)-5(d)(1) and (3)): the beneficiary's, at her age on her birthday in the year after the death, less 1 for each year since; or the owner's, at his age on his birthday in the year he died, less 1 for each year since. The Uniform Lifetime Table and the joint table are never used for an inherited IRA. Harborline rounds to the cent.

A missed RMD is corrected by distributing the shortfall from the account that owed it: for an inherited IRA, from that inherited IRA (or another inherited from the same person), never from an IRA she owns (Treas. Reg. 54.4974-1(a)(2); 1.408-8(e)). The tax is 25% of the shortfall, or 10% if the shortfall is distributed within the correction window and a return reflecting the tax is filed; the window ends at the earliest of a notice of deficiency, an assessment, or the last day of the second taxable year after the year of the tax, so 31 December 2027 for a 2025 RMD (IRC 4974(a) and (e)). The IRS may waive the tax for reasonable error with reasonable steps to remedy it (IRC 4974(d); Form 5329). A corrective distribution does not count toward the year it is taken in: that year's own RMD is taken as well (the IRS's proposed rule, 89 FR 58644, which Harborline applies as a good-faith reading).

Only a surviving spouse who is the sole beneficiary may treat an inherited IRA as her own (Treas. Reg. 1.408-8(c)). No other beneficiary may: a brother's or sister's IRA stays an inherited IRA, under the beneficiary rules, until it is empty. Harborline's treat-as-own election is for spouses only.

documents.title: IRS Instructions for Form 5329 (2025), Part IX, saved by Wexley & Marr
documents.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026. The tax is due for the tax year that includes the last day by which the RMD must be taken. Lines 52a and 53a: plans whose shortfall was distributed in full during the correction window; 52b and 53b: all other plans. Line 53 does not include a distribution received after the deadline or during the correction window. Line 54a is 10% of its shortfall, 54b 25%. The 10% rate needs the shortfall distributed from the plan for which the tax was imposed, during the correction window, and a return reflecting the tax. Waiver of tax for reasonable cause: the IRS can waive part or all of the tax if the shortfall was due to reasonable error and you are taking reasonable steps to remedy it. Attach a statement of explanation, enter "RC" and the amount you want waived in parentheses next to line 54a and/or 54b, subtract it from the shortfall, enter the result there, and complete line 55. Pay any tax reported on line 55. If the IRS does not grant the waiver, it notifies you of any tax owed.
